common_name: Garrett's California Fuchsia (Great Basin Hummingbird Trumpet)

planting.note: Divide rhizomatous clumps or sow stratified seed in fall into gravelly, fast-draining soil; withhold summer water and shear top growth back hard in late winter before new shoots emerge.

directions: This is the cold-hardy, interior-Great-Basin race of California fuchsia, native to montane Utah, southeastern Idaho, and northwestern Wyoming rather than coastal California, bringing the species' late-season hummingbird bloom to intermountain-climate gardens where the coastal subspecies would not reliably overwinter. It tolerates far colder, drier winter conditions than typical nursery California fuchsia and is prone to crown rot in heavy or regularly irrigated soils. It spreads by shallow rhizomes into a loose mat, so site it where it can wander along a dry slope rather than in a tight formal border.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall into sharply drained rocky soil; let it run as a loosely spreading groundcover along a bank rather than a tidy clump.

directions: A higher-elevation Sierra Nevada and desert-mountain race with broader, more strongly silvered foliage than coastal forms, this subspecies offers a bolder foliage texture alongside the fall hummingbird bloom. It occurs naturally on dry, rocky ridges from roughly 1,600 to nearly 10,000 feet, so it wants sharp drainage and resents both summer irrigation and heavy clay. Let its silvery mass and late-season orange-red trumpets be appreciated from a distance along a bank.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant in fall into alkaline, fast-draining soil near the coast; avoid acidic amendments or peat-based mixes, and cut back hard after bloom.

directions: The most geographically restricted subspecies, confined to coastal sage scrub and chaparral slopes below about 2,000 feet near the Southern California coast, this fuchsia offers a lower-growing, fine-textured, linear-silver-leafed form suited to compact coastal gardens and alkaline soils where the taller subspecies would look out of scale. Because its native range is so narrowly coastal, it is best reserved for true coastal or near-coastal gardens rather than inland heat.

planting.note: Sow in spring into an ordinary well-drained rock-garden scree mix; keep on the dry side between waterings.

directions: A compact, woody-caudexed rock-garden perennial endemic to the Klamath Mountains' serpentine outcrops, this species carries heart-shaped bright pink flowers in a genuinely distinct growth form from the shrubby California fuchsias, suited to scree beds, raised alpine troughs, and difficult serpentine or ultramafic garden soils where little else thrives. It tolerates low-nutrient, often magnesium-heavy conditions that defeat most garden perennials, forming a tight clump of tough, peeling stems radiating from a woody base.

planting.note: Press seed onto the soil surface without burying, since it needs light to germinate, into a rain garden, pond margin, or seasonally flooded swale.

directions: A widespread, fast-growing native wetland perennial with deeply notched pink-to-white veined flowers, this willowherb wants the opposite conditions from California fuchsia — consistently moist to wet, organically rich soil — and will self-sow readily once established, so give it room to naturalize. Its tall, somewhat gangly habit and bristly-glandular stems tuck easily behind shorter wetland companions, adding a long midsummer bloom window. It spreads both by wind-borne seed and overwintering basal rosettes.

subcategory: vernal pool and rain garden annual

planting.note: Scatter seed directly on bare, disturbed soil in fall or winter without transplanting, into a site wet through winter and spring that dries by summer.

directions: A fast-growing native annual of seasonally wet ground that reliably self-sows in rain gardens, bioswales, and vernal-pool-style plantings without irrigation, this species offers a dense, hairy pink-and-white flower spike plus genuine ecological value — its seed feeds breeding goldfinches and it hosts the bedstraw hawkmoth, a hummingbird-mimicking pollinator. It should not be kept artificially moist once it has set seed, since it is adapted to the classic vernal-pool wet-winter, dry-summer cycle.
